title: Bigger Hands, Snoring and Sweats / Measure IGF-1, Not a Random Growth Hormone

blocks.text: Bigger Hands, Snoring and Sweats / Measure IGF-1, Not a Random Growth Hormone

AMaC MRCP PACES · X-06 · Consultation · PACES Consultation (Station 5) · Skills A, B, C, D, E, F, G · 20 minutes (15 with the patient, then 5 of examiner questions; warning at 13 minutes) · Guidelines: Acromegaly Consensus Group: Consensus on criteria for acromegaly diagnosis and remission (Pituitary 2024;27:7-22; published online November 2023); Endocrine Society acromegaly clinical practice guideline (2014), for treatment; DVLA: Miscellaneous conditions, assessing fitness to drive (last updated 7 November 2025) · Related AMaC: None identified

Dear Doctor, a 49-year-old joiner. A year of bigger hands and feet, sweating, loud snoring and aching joints. He fell asleep at the wheel of his van last month. Blood pressure 150/94. A random growth hormone was reported as normal. Please assess and advise.
The patient has consented to see you. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to the patient.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. Enlarging hands and feet, sweating, snoring and joint pain points to acromegaly. A normal random growth hormone does not exclude it, and a sleepy van driver is a danger today.

The Examiner Trap. He is reassured by the normal growth hormone and does not want to stop work. Candidates agree it is normal, or forget his driving. Pass: IGF-1 (clearly raised confirms it), glucose tolerance test if equivocal, MRI, no driving while sleepy. Fail: random GH accepted, or driving allowed.

rows: Ask about the changes, then ask about sleep, sweating, vision and driving.
"What has changed in your hands, feet or face? How do you sleep? Do you fall asleep driving?"
Rings and shoes; sweating; headaches; vision; snoring; sleepiness; driving; joints; carpal tunnel; sexual function.
Look at the hands, face and jaw, test the fields, and check the blood pressure.
"May I look at your hands, face and mouth, test your sight at the edges and check your blood pressure? Tell me if anything hurts."
Hands; spade shape; face; jaw; tongue; fields; fundi; Tinel; blood pressure; goitre; cover him.
Explain what you suspect, the right test, why it matters, and the safe advice about driving.
"I think a gland in your head is making too much growth hormone. A random level can miss it. Please don't drive while sleepy."
IGF-1; glucose test if equivocal; MRI; sleep; driving; treatment; follow-up.
No introduction or consent; examines without asking; leaves him exposed.
Introduces self, asks consent, asks about discomfort before examining, covers him and thanks him.
Also offers a chaperone and asks permission before examining the mouth and neck.
Asks about hands only; omits sleep, sweating, vision or driving.
Asks ring and shoe size, sweating, headache, vision, snoring, sleepiness, driving, joint pain, carpal tunnel and sexual function.
Also asks about weight change, old photographs, family history and previous colon problems.
Omits the visual fields or the hands; reports field loss that is absent.
Finds large spade-like hands, coarse features, prominent jaw, large tongue, positive Tinel sign, normal fields and blood pressure 150/94.
Also finds oily skin, skin tags, a normal thyroid and normal fundi.
Acromegaly from a pituitary adenoma, with sleep apnoea.
Also names Paget disease, hypothyroidism and pachydermoperiostosis, and says old photographs help.
Relies on a random growth hormone, or orders a scan first.
Asks for IGF-1 (with typical features, above 1.3 times the upper limit for age confirms it), a glucose tolerance test with growth hormone if equivocal, a pituitary MRI, and other pituitary hormones.
Also asks for a sleep study, HbA1c and echocardiography, and says glucose control and the assay affect how a glucose tolerance test is read.
Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): says he can keep driving his van while sleepy, or accepts the random growth hormone as normal.
Says no driving while sleepy, and that he must tell DVLA if moderate or severe sleep apnoea is confirmed; surgery is first-line; medical therapy if disease persists.
Also names somatostatin analogues, pegvisomant and cabergoline, and an age-normal IGF-1 as the target.
Brushes aside his fear for his job and his hands.
Asks what worries him, acknowledges both and explains treatment can reduce the symptoms.
Also offers a letter for work and discusses the effect on his income.
Tells him what to do with no choices.
Explains tests and surgical referral, or tests with medical treatment first, and asks his choice.
Records his choice, gives a written plan and a dated review.

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail.
Who you are: A 49-year-old self-employed joiner. You are cheerful, stubborn and worried about money.
Opening line: "My hands have got huge, my wedding ring won't come off, I sweat like a pig and my wife says I snore like a train."
Volunteered: one year. Shoe size up two sizes. Aching knees and hands.

Only if asked: tingling in both hands at night. A dull headache most days. No change in vision. Libido is a bit lower. No regular tablets. No allergies. Never smoked. Two pints at weekends. No recent travel. No family history of pituitary problems.
Only if asked about driving: you fell asleep at the wheel last month and woke on the verge. You drive your van every day.
Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): you are afraid you will lose your job and the house if you cannot drive. Say: "If I can't drive, I can't work."
Your questions, in your own words: "Is it serious?" "Is it a tumour?" "Can I carry on driving?"
How you react: if told to stop driving with no help, you refuse. If listened to and offered a letter and a plan, you agree. If offered options, you choose.

Findings, released when examined: comfortable; pulse 78 regular; blood pressure 150/94; temperature 36.7 °C. Large spade-like hands; coarse features; prominent jaw; large tongue; oily skin; skin tags. Positive Tinel sign. Visual fields normal. Fundi normal. Thyroid normal.

Results, only when requested: IGF-1 3.2 times the upper limit of normal for age (scenario value), enough to confirm the diagnosis with these features; if a glucose tolerance test is requested, growth hormone nadir 2.1 microgram/litre, not suppressed, read with caution because HbA1c is 56 mmol/mol (diabetic range); prolactin normal. MRI: a pituitary macroadenoma not touching the chiasm. Sleep study: moderate obstructive sleep apnoea.
Question ladder: 1. Diagnosis? (D) 2. Why is a random growth hormone not enough? (D) 3. Which tests? (E) 4. What is first-line treatment? (E) 5. What do you tell him about driving? (E)

Curveballs: He says he will carry on driving: no; he must tell DVLA if moderate or severe sleep apnoea is confirmed. He asks about tablets rather than surgery: medical therapy if disease persists. Sudden severe headache and visual loss: emergency.
Introduces self, asks consent and asks about discomfort before examining (G)
Asks about sleep, sweating, vision and driving (C)
Tests the visual fields and checks the hands and jaw (A)
Finds spade-like hands, coarse features, large tongue and a positive Tinel sign (B)
Names acromegaly from a pituitary adenoma, with sleep apnoea (D)
Requests IGF-1, with a glucose tolerance test if equivocal, not a random growth hormone (E)
Requests pituitary MRI and other pituitary hormones (E)
Says no driving while sleepy and that he must tell DVLA if moderate or severe sleep apnoea is confirmed (E)
Names transsphenoidal surgery first-line and medical options (E)
Asks what worries him and offers a letter for work (F)
Fail performance
CANDIDATE: Take your shirt off. [R1 Fail] Hands big? [R2 Fail]
CANDIDATE: (Skips the fields.) [R3 Fail] It's obesity. [R4 Fail] The growth hormone was normal, so nothing to test. [R5 Fail]
CANDIDATE: Carry on driving; you need to work. [R6 Fail] Nothing to worry about. [R7 Fail] Come back in a year. [R8 Fail]

Examiner note: Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): a man who fell asleep at the wheel must not drive while sleepy. No consent, fields skipped, and the diagnosis missed on a random result.
Pass performance

CANDIDATE: (Cleans hands.) I'm the registrar. May I look at your hands and face, test your sight at the edges and check your blood pressure? Tell me if anything hurts. I'll cover you afterwards. [R1 Pass]
CANDIDATE: Any sweating, headaches, vision change, snoring or sleepiness? Do you drive? [R2 Pass]
PATIENT: Sweats, snoring. I fell asleep at the wheel last month.
CANDIDATE: (Examines.) Large spade-like hands, coarse features, prominent jaw, large tongue, positive Tinel sign, normal fields, blood pressure 150/94. [R3 Pass]
CANDIDATE: Acromegaly from a pituitary tumour, probably with sleep apnoea. [R4 Pass]

CANDIDATE: A random growth hormone isn't enough. I'll check IGF-1; with these features a clearly raised level confirms it, and a glucose tolerance test helps if it is borderline. Then an MRI and the other pituitary hormones. [R5 Pass]
CANDIDATE: Don't drive while sleepy, and you must tell DVLA if moderate or severe sleep apnoea is confirmed. Surgery is first-line. [R6 Pass]
CANDIDATE: What worries you? [R7 Pass]
PATIENT: My job and the house.
CANDIDATE: That is fair; with your permission I'll write a letter for work. [R7 Pass] We can book tests and surgery review, or tests with tablets first. Which do you prefer? [R8 Pass]
Examiner note: Diagnosed it and gave driving advice. Did not name the differential or the medical options and IGF-1 target.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: I'm the registrar. May I examine you? Would you like a chaperone? I'll ask before looking in your mouth and at your neck. [R1 High]
CANDIDATE: Any old photographs, weight change or family history? Any carpal tunnel symptoms? [R2 High]
CANDIDATE: (Examines.) Oily skin, skin tags, normal thyroid, normal fundi. [R3 High]
CANDIDATE: Acromegaly; Paget disease, hypothyroidism and pachydermoperiostosis are less likely, and old photographs help. [R4 High]

CANDIDATE: IGF-1 against the upper limit for age; a glucose tolerance test only if equivocal, read with his glucose control and the assay in mind; MRI, other pituitary hormones, a sleep study, HbA1c and echo. [R5 High]
CANDIDATE: No driving until sleepiness is controlled. Surgery first; then somatostatin analogues, pegvisomant or cabergoline, aiming for an age-normal IGF-1. [R6 High]
CANDIDATE: With your permission I'll write a letter for your work, and we can discuss your income. [R7 High]
CANDIDATE: I'll give you a written plan and review you with the results. [R8 High]
Examiner note: Added a chaperone, wider history, differentials, the full investigation set, medical options and IGF-1 target, a letter for work and a written plan.
R3: Not testing the visual fields. A pituitary tumour can compress the chiasm, and missed field loss changes the urgency.
R5: Relying on a random growth hormone. It does not exclude acromegaly, and IGF-1 is the test.
R6: Letting him keep driving. He has already fallen asleep at the wheel.
R7: Ignoring his job. He will keep driving if no practical help is offered.
"May I test the visual fields before I go on?"
"A random growth hormone isn't enough; I'd measure IGF-1."
"I'd like to check I've understood what worries you most."

Acromegaly consensus (Pituitary 2024): with typical features, IGF-1 above 1.3 times the upper limit of normal for age confirms acromegaly; random growth hormone is not needed. Use a 75 g glucose tolerance test (growth hormone at 0, 30, 60, 90 and 120 minutes) when the diagnosis is equivocal; BMI-based nadir cut-offs (below 0.4 microgram/litre if BMI is under 25, below 0.2 if 25 or more) are assay-dependent, and uncontrolled diabetes makes results less reliable. The older Endocrine Society 2014 cut-off was a nadir below 1 microgram/litre.

MRI is the imaging modality of choice. Transsphenoidal surgery is first-line in most; medical therapy if disease persists. Evaluate for hypertension, diabetes, cardiovascular disease and sleep apnoea. Target: age-normal IGF-1.
DVLA (Group 1 and Group 2; last updated 7 November 2025): suspected sleep apnoea, no driving until symptoms are controlled; moderate or severe, the driver must notify DVLA.
THINK: Big hands, sweats, snoring: acromegaly.
SAY: "A gland in your head makes too much growth hormone."
DO: Test fields; ask about driving.
NUMBERS: IGF-1 above 1.3 times upper limit for age confirms; glucose test only if equivocal (Pituitary 2024).
TRAP: Random growth hormone; driving.
FINISH: IGF-1, glucose test if equivocal, MRI, surgery first, no driving.

Katznelson L et al. Acromegaly: an Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline (2014). https://academic.oup.com/jcem/article/99/11/3933/2836347 Supports: MRI, surgery and medical therapy, comorbidities and IGF-1 target (diagnostic criteria superseded by the 2024 consensus).

Giustina A, Biermasz N, Casanueva FF, et al. Consensus on criteria for acromegaly diagnosis and remission. Pituitary 2024;27:7-22. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11102-023-01360-1 Supports: IGF-1 above 1.3 times the upper limit for age confirms the diagnosis with typical features; random growth hormone not required; glucose tolerance test for equivocal cases, with BMI-based nadir cut-offs and caution in uncontrolled diabetes.

DVLA. Miscellaneous conditions: assessing fitness to drive (last updated 7 November 2025). https://www.gov.uk/guidance/miscellaneous-conditions-assessing-fitness-to-drive Supports: Sleepiness and obstructive sleep apnoea rules for Group 1 and Group 2.
